Synchros use a single energized rotating primary winding on the rotor and three stationary secondary windings on the stator. The combination used ensures only one voltage combination for any position in the rotation of the rotor.

Since one side of the secondary windings are common, the three outputs are each a combination of two adjacent secondary windings. When the two windings are in phase the output voltage is added. This would be when the output voltage is increasing during rotation.

When the adjacent windings are out of phase due to the rotation of the primary, the voltage is decreasing at the output. . The combination used ensures only one voltage combination for any position in the rotation of the rotor...
The AC voltage developed at three windings in the secondary remains constant as long as the rotor remains in one position and varies with the slightest movement of the rotor.

Of course, all this rotation control means nothing unless something can be done with it. This is where the synchronization comes in. We've been reviewing the transmitter portion of a simple synchro system. Review the schematic diagram while reading the following pages.

The simplest synchro system consists of a transmitter and a receiver. The rotor for both the transmitter and the receiver are driven from the same single phase AC source and stay in constant phase regardless of the rotational position.

The stator windings are paralleled between the transmitter and receiver. S1 S2 and S3 of the transmitter are tied to S1, S2 and S3 of the receiver. Notice that the voltages at S1, S2 and S3 are at equal potentials with no current flow. This is called correspondence.

When the TX rotor is moved, S1 has the strongest magnetic field and largest current flow while current and voltage potential in S2 has decreased. There is now a difference in stator potentials between the TX and the TR... voltage relationship of the stator windings.

The simple synchro system we've used thus far is called a Torque Synchro. Another form of synchro is the Control Synchro. This is the schematic symbol for both types.
Torque synchros provide a mechanical output and are used in synchro systems with a light load.

Torque synchros are well suited for tasks such as positioning indicator dials on instrument panels.
Control synchros provide an electrical output and are used in synchro systems with a heavy load.
Control synchros can be used to position radars and other heavy equipment.
